lead: Liquid–liquid extraction pulls a solute out of a liquid feed with a second liquid solvent. Add solvent, mix, let layers settle; solute divides between them. It works when distillation fails: components boil too close, or solute decomposes at its boiling point. It recovers acetic acid from dilute water, purifies antibiotics, separates metals. A triangular diagram gives equilibrium compositions, so stages can be sized.
prereq: You need the equilibrium stage and stage efficiency from Unit 2, and the distribution coefficient.

sections.h3: Solute, carrier and solvent: naming the three players

blocks.text: Extraction moves solute A from liquid feed into added solvent S. Carrier B, also called diluent, is the rest of the feed and stays behind. Mix S with feed; A partly leaves B and enters S. The mixture splits into two layers. Extract is rich in S and A. Raffinate is rich in B, holding some A. Settle, draw off layers, recover A from extract (usually by distillation), return S.
Transfer stops at equilibrium, when the layers hold A in a fixed ratio. Each stage is one mix-and-settle.

items: Selectivity: S dissolves much more A than B. Equal uptake only dilutes feed.
Distribution coefficient away from 1, so each kilogram of solvent carries useful load.
Density difference of about 50 kg/m³ or more between saturated layers, or droplets settle slowly.
Interfacial tension high enough for droplets to coalesce after mixing, low enough to redisperse easily.
Low mutual solubility of S and B, so solvent is not lost and extract is not diluted.
Low viscosity; boiling point well separated from A; cheap, non-corrosive, low toxicity, non-flammable.

sections.h3: The equilateral triangle: one point, one mixture

blocks.text: Three fractions sum to 1, so two are independent. The equilateral triangle holds them: pure A at top, pure B at bottom left, pure S at bottom right. Some syllabi call it a Gibbs triangle. Every mixture has one point inside.

items: Mass fraction of A at point P: perpendicular from P to B–S side divided by triangle height.
Mass fraction of B: perpendicular to A–S side.
Mass fraction of S: perpendicular to A–B side.
The three fractions add to 1. Reading along grid lines parallel to the sides gives the same numbers.

blocks.text: The binodal curve, or solubility curve, is the boundary. Outside it near the corners is single-phase: one liquid, no split. Inside is two-phase, splitting into layers at the ends of the tie line through the point. Tie lines slope on the equilateral triangle and on a right-angled ternary plot. Horizontal lines are constant A, not tie lines. Only the y-versus-x distribution plot collapses a tie line to a point. Tie lines shorten to the plait point, where layers become identical.

Type 1: one pair, usually B and S, is partly miscible; common case with a plait point, as in water–acetic acid–ether. Type 2: two pairs are partly miscible; two two-phase regions. Type 3: all three pairs are partly miscible; three two-phase regions and a small three-phase region in the middle.

sections.h3: Distribution coefficient and solute-free mass ratios

blocks.text: At fixed temperature the layers hold A in a fixed ratio. On a mass-fraction basis, K = y/x, where y is mass fraction of A in extract and x is mass fraction of A in raffinate.

blocks.where: K is the distribution coefficient (dimensionless); y is kg A per kg extract; x is kg A per kg raffinate; both layers are at the same temperature and in equilibrium.

blocks.text: K is not constant. It drifts with composition because tie lines are not parallel, and changes with temperature. Use one K only where tie lines are nearly parallel; otherwise step stages on the diagram (see 5.3).

blocks.where: X is kg A per kg carrier B in the raffinate; Y is kg A per kg solvent S in the extract; x and y are mass fractions of A in raffinate and extract. Valid when raffinate is nearly A + B and extract nearly A + S.

blocks.text: Solute-free ratios help because B stays in raffinate and S in extract. Balances in X and Y give straight operating lines, so many designs plot X against Y (repeated stages: 5.2). Here x = 0.0667 gives X = 0.0714 kg acid per kg water; y = 0.20 gives Y = 0.25 kg acid per kg ether.

figure.caption: Solute A is present in both layers at equilibrium. The carrier stays mostly in the raffinate and the solvent mostly in the extract, which is why each layer is named after the liquid that dominates it.

spec.aria: Two settled liquid layers, the carrier-rich raffinate and the solvent-rich extract, each holding solute A at equilibrium.

examples.question: One equilibrium stage contacts 100 kg/h feed with 30 mass% acetic acid (A) in water (B) with 100 kg/h pure ether (S). Neglect mutual solubility. At equilibrium raffinate has 6.67 mass% acid; extract has 20.0 mass% acid. Find layer flows, acid recovered, percentage recovery, and K.
steps: Basis 1 h. Feed acid = 0.30 × 100 = 30 kg. Feed water = 0.70 × 100 = 70 kg. Solvent ether = 100 kg, no acid.
Water only in raffinate: 0.9333 × R = 70 kg, so R = 75.0 kg/h. R is raffinate mass flow.
Ether only in extract: 0.800 × E = 100 kg, so E = 125.0 kg/h. E is extract mass flow.
Acid in raffinate = 0.0667 × 75.0 = 5.0 kg/h. Acid in extract = 0.200 × 125.0 = 25.0 kg/h. Sum = 30.0 kg/h.
Recovery = acid in extract / acid in feed = 25.0 / 30.0 = 0.8333, that is 83.33 %.
Solute-free ratios: X = 0.0667 / 0.9333 = 0.0714 kg acid per kg water; Y = 0.200 / 0.800 = 0.250 kg acid per kg ether.
examples.answer: Raffinate 75.0 kg/h, extract 125.0 kg/h, 25.0 kg/h acid recovered (83.33 %), and K = 3.0.
examples.check:
F = 100.0
xF = 0.30
S = 100.0
y = 0.20
x = 1.0/15.0
water = F*(1-xF)
R = water/(1-x)
E = S/(1-y)
acid_ext = y*E
acid_feed = F*xF
rec = acid_ext/acid_feed*100
K = y/x
print(round(R,2))
print(round(E,2))
print(round(acid_ext,2))
print(round(rec,2))
print(round(K,2))

traps: Tie lines slope on the equilateral triangle and on a right-angled ternary plot. Horizontal lines are constant A, not tie lines. Only the y-versus-x plot collapses each tie line to a point.
K uses mass fractions of the whole layer. A solute-free ratio such as Y/X gives a different number; here K = 3.0 but Y/X = 3.5.
Extract is solvent-rich and raffinate carrier-rich. Swapping them reverses every balance.
Neglecting mutual solubility must be justified. If solvent dissolves carrier, the simple balances break down and the full ternary diagram is needed.
The plait point is where phases become identical, not the richest extract. Beyond it there is one phase and no separation.

quiz.q: Define solute, carrier, solvent, extract and raffinate in one line each.
quiz.a: Solute A is the component being moved. Carrier B (diluent) is the rest of the feed. Solvent S is the added liquid that dissolves A. Extract is the solvent-rich layer leaving the stage. Raffinate is the carrier-rich layer left behind.

quiz.q: Why does a mixture whose point lies outside the binodal curve not split into two layers?
quiz.a: Outside the curve the mixture is one stable liquid phase. A split requires the overall composition to sit on a tie line joining two binodal points. No tie line passes through a point outside the curve, so one phase is the only state.

quiz.q: A raffinate holds 10 mass% solute and the extract holds 30 mass%. Find K on a mass-fraction basis and the solute-free ratios X and Y.
quiz.a: K = y/x = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0. X = 0.10/0.90 = 0.111 kg solute per kg carrier. Y = 0.30/0.70 = 0.429 kg solute per kg solvent. Y/X = 3.86, not 3.0.

quiz.q: 100 kg/h of a 20 mass% solution in carrier B is extracted in one stage with 150 kg/h pure solvent S. Neglect mutual solubility; extract contains 10 mass% solute. Find raffinate mass and percentage recovery.
quiz.a: Solute in feed = 20 kg, carrier = 80 kg. Solvent in extract = 0.90 × E = 150, so E = 166.67 kg/h and solute in extract = 16.67 kg. Raffinate solute = 20 − 16.67 = 3.33 kg; raffinate mass = 80 + 3.33 = 83.33 kg/h. Recovery = 16.67/20 = 83.3 %.

quiz.q: A student reads a point in the two-phase region, draws a horizontal line to the other branch of the curve, and calls it the tie line. What is wrong and what error follows?
quiz.a: A horizontal line on a ternary plot is constant A, not a tie line. Tie lines slope on both plots. The true tie line joins the two equilibrium compositions on the curve. The horizontal guess gives wrong extract composition, hence wrong y, K and recovery.

quiz.q: Two solvents give the same K for the solute but differ in how much carrier they dissolve. Which do you choose and why?
quiz.a: Choose the one with lower mutual solubility of carrier. Less carrier in extract gives purer extract and cheaper solute–solvent separation; less solvent in raffinate means less make-up and cheaper recovery. Equal K means equal solvent flow, so decide on solubility, density difference and cost.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial extraction handles copper and rare-earth purification, antibiotics, and nuclear fuel reprocessing with tributyl phosphate. Modern design predicts K and the binodal curve from group-contribution or quantum-solvent models instead of measuring every tie line. Solvent-selection guides screen candidates for toxicity and boiling point. Supercritical carbon dioxide and ionic liquids appear where residues or flammability matter. Search liquid–liquid equilibrium data compilations, UNIFAC, and pharmaceutical solvent selection guides.
